definition: A modest view of your own importance, free of pride or arrogance.
example: After winning the prize, the scientist spoke with humility about how much her lab assistants had contributed.
nuance: Humility is a modesty a person chooses, while humiliation is a painful shame that others force on someone.
prompt: A chess champion is interviewed right after winning a close final match.
options: With humility, she credited her coach and said her rival had nearly won.
Her humility came from the crowd mocking her early mistakes.
Showing humility, she announced that no player alive could ever beat her.
The humility in the crowded hall made everyone's shirts damp with sweat.
reasons: Sharing credit and admitting the win was close shows a modest sense of her own importance.
Being mocked by others causes humiliation, which is a different word from humility.
Boasting that she is unbeatable is arrogance, the opposite of a modest attitude.
This mixes up humility with humidity, the moisture in the air.

practice.prompt: A new employee joins a team of experienced engineers.
options: Out of humility, he rewrote everyone's code without asking, sure his was best.
He suffered terrible humility when his manager scolded him in front of the team.
His humility made his hands shake so badly he dropped his notes during meetings.
His humility showed when he asked senior colleagues to review his first design.
reasons: Assuming his work beats everyone else's is overconfidence, not modesty.
Public scolding causes humiliation; nobody 'suffers' humility because it is a chosen attitude.
Shaking hands point to nerves or fear, which is not the same as a modest view of oneself.
Asking more experienced people to check his work shows he doesn't overrate himself.
